nahhas-meani:1-1.t:
Among what we set out to treat is His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿بِسْمِ ٱللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيـمِ﴾
Most of the Basrans said: The meaning is: "The first thing with which I begin is "بسم اللهِ", and the first of my speech is "بِسمِ اللهِ"."
Sībawayh said: The meaning of the bāʾ is ilṣāq (attachment/adhesion).
Al-Farrāʾ said: The position of the bāʾ is accusative (manṣūb), and the meaning is: "I have begun with the name of Allah," and "I begin with the name of Allah."
Concerning the derivation of "اسم" there are two views:
One of them: it is from al-sumuww, which is elevation and height; it was called "اسم" because its bearer is, as it were, raised up by it.
And it was said: it is from wasamtu (I marked); it was called "اسم" because it is to its bearer like a mark (sima), i.e. he is known by it.
The second view is mistaken, because what has dropped from it is its lām (final radical), so it is established that it is from samā yasmū.
Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā said: One says sim and sam, and one says ism with a kasra on the alif, and one says it with a ḍamma.
Whoever puts a ḍamma on the alif takes it from samawtu asmū.
And whoever puts a kasra takes it from samaytu asmī.
Al-Kisāʾī and al-Farrāʾ said: The meaning of "بسمِ اللهِ" is "in the name of al-ilāh (the deity)"; they dropped the hamza and assimilated the first lām into the second, so it became a doubled lām, just as He, Majestic and Mighty, said: ﴿لَّٰكِنَّاْ هُوَ ٱللَّهُ رَبِّي﴾, whose meaning is: "لَكِنْ أَنَا هُوَ اللهُ رَبِّي"; that is how al-Ḥasan read it.
Sībawayh has two views on this:
One of them: that the origin is ilāh, then the alif and lām were brought in as a substitute (ʿiwaḍ) for the hamza; likewise al-nās, in his view, has the origin unās.
The other view — which is also the view of his followers — is that the origin is lāh, then the alif and lām entered upon it; and they cited:
لاَهِ ابنُ عَمِّكَ لاَ أَفْضَلْتَ فِي حَسَبٍ * عَنِّي وَلاَ أَنْتَ دَيَّانِي فَتَخْزُونِي
(For God's sake [i.e. by God], your cousin — you do not surpass me in lineage, nor are you my master that you should govern me.)
And one asks about the repetition in His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيـمِ﴾.
It is related from Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: ﴿الرَّحْمٰنُ الرَّحِيـمُ﴾ are two gentle names, one of them gentler than the other: al-Raḥmān is the Gentle, and al-Raḥīm is the One who is kind to His creation with provision.
Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī said: "الرَّحمنُ" towards His creation, "الرحيم" towards His servants in the honour and proof with which He initiated them.
ʿAṭāʾ al-Khurāsānī said: He was al-Raḥmān; then when al-Raḥmān was appropriated from among His names, it became "al-Raḥmān al-Raḥīm". [Translator's note: the source writes «الخرساني» and «اختزل»; the sense appears to be that the name al-Raḥmān was usurped (by Musaylima, as reported elsewhere), so al-Raḥīm was added; translated as written.]
Al-ʿArzamī said: "الرحمن" towards all creation, "الرحيم" towards the believers.
Abū ʿUbayda said: Both are from al-raḥma (mercy), like their saying nadmān and nadīm (boon companion).
Quṭrub said: It is possible that the two were joined together for tawkīd (emphasis). This is a good view; in emphasis there is the greatest benefit, and it is abundant in the speech of the Arabs, needing no supporting citation.
The benefit in that is what Muḥammad ibn Yazīd said: that it is favour after favour, and bounty after bounty, a strengthening of the hopes of those who call upon Him, and a promise whose hoper is not disappointed.
The view of al-ʿArzamī is also good, because the pattern "fa'lān" contains the meaning of intensiveness (mubālagha); so it is as if — and Allah knows best — He is al-Raḥmān towards all His creation, and for this reason it is applied only to Allah the Exalted, because its meaning is: the One whose mercy encompasses everything.
And for this reason it was placed before "الرحيم".
And "الرحيم" became preferable to al-rāḥim (the one showing mercy), because "الرحيم" is more binding in praise, since it indicates that mercy is permanent in Him, never departing, whereas al-rāḥim applies to one who has shown mercy a single time.
Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā said: "الرحيم" is Arabic and "الرَّحْمَن" is Hebrew, and for this reason the two were joined.
This view is to be turned away from.
Maṭar related from Qatāda concerning His saying ﴿بِسْمِ ٱللهِ الرَّحْمٰنِ الرَّحِيـمِ﴾ that he said: He praised Himself. And this is a good view.
Abū al-ʿAbbās said: The naʿt (adjective) may occur for praise, as when you say: "Jarīr the poet said."

nahhas-meani:2-2.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ٱلْحَمْدُ للَّهِ﴾. The difference between al-ḥamd (praise) and al-shukr (thanks) is that al-ḥamd is more general, because it applies to commendation (thanāʾ), to glorification (taḥmīd), and to thanks and requital.
Al-shukr is restricted to what is a recompense to one who has done you a kindness; so al-ḥamd is more firmly established in the verse, because it goes beyond thanks.
And it is said: al-ḥamd is a khabar (statement/predication), and the way of a statement is to convey information; so what is the benefit in this?
The answer to this is that Sībawayh said: When a man says "الحمدُ للهِ" with the nominative, it carries the same meaning as his saying "حمدتُ اللهَ حمداً" (I have praised Allah with praise), except that the one who puts al-ḥamd in the nominative states that praise — from him and from all creation — belongs to Allah the Exalted, while the one who puts al-ḥamd in the accusative states that praise from him alone is to Allah the Exalted.
Ibn Kaysān said: This is very good speech, because your saying "الحمدُ للهِ" has the same grammatical form as your saying "المالُ لزيدٍ" (the wealth belongs to Zayd), and its meaning is that you have stated it while intending to be one who praises, not one who reports something; so in the speaker's stating this there is an acknowledgment from him that Allah the Exalted is entitled to it from His creation; thus he is the most praising of those who praise Him, since he acknowledges that praise belongs to Him. So the meaning of the nominative comes back to the same as the meaning of the accusative, and exceeds it in that he has made the praise that comes from his own act and the act of others belong to Allah the Exalted.
Someone other than Sībawayh said: This is spoken only as a seeking of the pardon and forgiveness of Allah the Exalted, and as an extolling and glorifying of Him; so it is contrary to the meaning of a statement, and contains the meaning of a request.
And in the ḥadīth: "Whoever is occupied with remembering Me from asking of Me, I shall give him the best of what I give those who ask."
And it was said: His praising of Himself, Majestic and Mighty, and His commending of Himself, is so that His servants may know that; so the meaning on this view is: Say: praise belongs to Allah.
The self-praise of a human being is only faulted because he is deficient: if he says "I am generous", there is stinginess there; and if he says "I am brave", there is cowardice there; and Allah the Exalted is free of that. For the human being praises himself only to gain a benefit or ward off harm, and Allah the Exalted has no need of this.
* And His saying, Majestic and Mighty: ﴿رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾.
The lexicographers said: al-rabb is the owner (al-mālik), and they cited:
وَهُوَ الرَبُّ والشَّهِيدُ عَلَى يَوْ * مِ الحِيَارَيْنِ وَالبَلاءُ بَلاَءُ
(And he is the lord and the witness over the day of al-Ḥiyārayn, and the trial was a [true] trial.)
The origin of this is that one says rabbahu, yarubbuhu, rabban, and he is rābb and rabb, when he undertakes its proper upkeep.
And one says, for intensiveness: rabbāhu, rabbabahu and rabbatahu.
ʿAṭāʾ ibn al-Sāʾib related from Saʿīd ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbās concerning ﴿رَبِّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ that he said: the jinn and humankind.
Al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas related from Abū al-ʿĀliya, who said: The jinn are a world (ʿālam), and humankind are a world, and besides that, the earth has four corners, in each corner one thousand five hundred worlds whom Allah created for His worship.
Abū ʿUbayda said: ﴿ربُّ ٱلْعَالَمِينَ﴾, i.e. of the created beings.
And al-ʿAjjāj recited: "فخندفٌ هامةُ هذا العالم" (So Khindif are the head of this world).
The first view is the most eminent of these views and the best known in the language, because this plural is the plural of rational beings specifically.
And "عالم" is derived from al-ʿalāma (sign).
Al-Khalīl said: al-ʿalam, al-ʿalāma and al-maʿlam are what indicate a thing; so the world (al-ʿālam) indicates that it has a Creator and Disposer.

nahhas-meani:4-4.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿مَلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ﴾, and it is also read ﴿مَـٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ﴾.
Abū Ḥātim chose (مَالكِ). He said: It is more comprehensive than (مَلِكِ), because you say: Allah is mālik (owner) of the people, mālik of the birds, mālik of the wind, and mālik of every single thing and every kind of thing; whereas one does not say: Allah is malik (king) of the birds, nor malik of the wind, and the like; "مَلِك" is only fitting with "the people" alone.
The eminent lexicographers disagreed with him in that, among them "Abū ʿUbayd" and Abū al-ʿAbbās "Muḥammad ibn Yazīd", and they argued from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿لِّمَنِ ٱلْمُلْكُ ٱلْيَوْمَ﴾? Al-mulk is the maṣdar (verbal noun) of al-malik, while the maṣdar of al-mālik is "milk" with a kasra; and this is a good argument.
Moreover, the argument of "Abū Ḥātim" is not binding, because "malik of the birds" and "of the winds" is not used only because there is no meaning of praise in it.
Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad narrated to us from Abū Dāwūd ibn al-Anbārī, who said: Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl narrated to us, saying: ʿAmr narrated to us from Asbāṭ from al-Suddī — he is Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Mālik [Translator's note: al-Suddī is usually named Ismāʿīl ibn ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Karīma; translated as written] — from Abū Mālik, and from Abū Ṣāliḥ from Ibn ʿAbbās, and from Murra al-Hamdānī from Ibn Masʿūd, and from people among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who said: ﴿مَـٰلِكِ يَوْمِ ٱلدِّينِ﴾: "the Day of al-Dīn" is the Day of Reckoning.
Mujāhid said: ﴿الدِّينُ﴾ is the requital (al-jazāʾ); and the two meanings are one, because the Day of Resurrection is the Day of Reckoning and the Day of Requital.
Al-dīn in other than this is obedience, and al-dīn is custom, as he said:
* أَهَذَا دِينُهُ أَبَداً ودِينِي"؟ *
(Is this ever to be his custom and mine?)
The meanings are close to one another, because when one obeys, one has submitted (dāna).
Custom runs the course of al-dīn; and "so-and-so is in the dīn of so-and-so" means: in his authority and obedience.
If it is said: Why was the Resurrection singled out for this?
The answer is: The Day of Resurrection is a day on which creatures are compelled to know that the whole matter belongs to Allah the Exalted.
And it was said: He singled it out because in this world there are kings and tyrants, while on the Day of Resurrection the whole matter returns to Allah the Exalted alone.

nahhas-meani:5-5.t:
His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿إِيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ﴾ — and He did not say "نَعْبُدكَ", because this is more emphatic.
Sībawayh said: It is as if they put first that whose clarification matters more to them and with whose clarification they are more concerned, even if both matter to them and concern them.
Worship (al-ʿibāda) in the language is obedience with abasement and submission. One says ṭarīq muʿabbad (a beaten road) when it has been made smooth by treading, and baʿīr muʿabbad (a tarred camel) when it has been smeared with tar, i.e. it has been put to menial use as a slave (ʿabd) is put to menial use. Ṭarafa said:
إلَى أَنْ تَحَامَتْنِي العَشِيرَةُ كُلُّهَا * وَأُفْرِدْتُ إفْرَادَ البَعِيرِ المعَبَّدِ
(Until the whole clan shunned me and I was set apart as the tarred camel is set apart.)
And one says ʿabida min kadhā, i.e. he disdained it, as the poet said:
* "وَأَعْبَدُ أَنْ تُهْجَى تَمِيمٌ بِدَارِمِ" *
(And I disdain that Tamīm be satirised by means of Dārim.)
* Then He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وإيَّاكَ نَسْتَعِينُ﴾.
He repeated "إيَّاكَ" for tawkīd (emphasis), and did not say "ونستعين", just as one says "the wealth is between Zayd and between ʿAmr", repeating "between" for emphasis. And He said ﴿إيَّاكَ﴾ and did not say "إيَّاه" (Him), because the meaning is: Say, O Muḥammad: "إيَّاكَ نَعْبُدُ".
Besides, the Arabs turn from the third person to direct address, as al-Aʿshā said:
عِنْدَهُ الحَزْمُ والتُّقَى وَأَسَى الصَرْ * عِ وَحَمْلٌ لمضْلِعِ الأَثْقَالِ
(With him are resolve, piety, consolation for the fallen, and the bearing of crushing burdens.)
Then he said, turning from the third person to address:
ووفاءٌ اذَا أَجَرْتَ فَما غُرَّ * تْ حبالٌ وصَلْتَها بحبالِ
(And faithfulness: when you grant protection, no ropes you have tied to [other] ropes are betrayed.)
And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَسَقَاهُمْ رَبُّهُمْ شَرَاباً طَهُوراً﴾.
Then He said: ﴿إنَّ هَذَا كَانَ لَكُمْ جَزَاءً﴾.
And the reverse of this: the Arabs turn from address to the third person, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿حَتَّىٰ إِذَا كُنتُمْ فِي ٱلْفُلْكِ وَجَرَيْنَ بِهِم بِرِيحٍ طَيِّبَةٍ﴾.
In the speech there is an omission, and the meaning is: and You alone we ask for help in that.

nahhas-meani:6-6.t:
He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَاطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾.
And they are already upon guidance, i.e. [the meaning is] make us firm, as you say to someone standing: "Stand until I come back to you", i.e. remain standing.
The meaning of ﴿ٱهْدِنَا﴾ is: guide us aright (arshidnā). The origin of hadā is arshada (to guide aright), and from it is: ﴿وَٱهْدِنَآ إِلَىٰ سَوَآءِ ٱلصِّرَاطِ﴾. Hadā may mean bayyana (to make clear), as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿وَأَمَّا ثَمُودُ فَهَدَيْنَاهُمْ﴾; and hadā may mean alhama (to inspire), as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿ٱلَّذِيۤ أَعْطَىٰ كُلَّ شَيءٍ خَلْقَهُ ثُمَّ هَدَىٰ﴾, i.e. He inspired it with what is good for it.
And it was said: [it means] approaching the female.
And hadā may mean daʿā (to call), as He said: ﴿وَلِكُلِّ قَوْمٍ هَادٍ﴾, i.e. a prophet who calls them.
The origin of all this is arshada; and the meaning is: guide us aright to the straight path.
Muḥammad ibn Jaʿfar al-Anbārī narrated to us, saying: Hāshim ibn al-Qāsim al-Ḥarrānī narrated to me, saying: Abū Isḥāq al-Naḥwī narrated to us from Ḥamza ibn Ḥabīb from Ḥumrān ibn Aʿyan from Abū Manṣūr, the nephew of al-Ḥārith, from al-Ḥārith from ʿAlī, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ say: "The straight path is the Book of Allah."
Misʿar related from Manṣūr from Abū Wāʾil from ʿAbd Allāh concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿ٱهْدِنَا ٱلصِّرَاطَ ٱلْمُسْتَقِيمَ﴾ that he said: The Book of Allah.
ʿAbd Allāh ibn Muḥammad ibn ʿAqīl related from Jābir, who said: It is Islam.
Al-ṣirāṭ in the language is the clear road; and the Book of Allah is like the clear road, and likewise Islam. Jarīr said:
أَمِيرُ المُؤمِنِينَ عَلَى صِرَاطٍ * إذا اعْوَجَّ المَوَارِدُ، مُسْتَقِيمِ
(The Commander of the Faithful is on a path that is straight when the watering-tracks go crooked.)
أَمِيرَ المُؤمِنِينَ جَمَعْتَ دِيناً * وَحِلْماً فَاضِلاً لِذَوِي الحُلُومِ
(O Commander of the Faithful, you have combined religion and a forbearance surpassing that of the forbearing.)
